tip: Θα σου αρέσει (tha su arési = it will please you) – liking works backwards: the island does the pleasing, you're on the receiving end.
Greek passes time instead of having it: θα περάσουμε τέλεια (tha perásume télia) is literally 'we'll pass perfectly' = we'll have a great time.
'On foot' is lit. 'with the feet': θα πάμε με τα πόδια (tha páme me ta pódhia = we'll go with the feet).
Countries wear the article: στην Ελλάδα (stin Elládha) – lit. 'to the Greece'. Greek normally puts 'the' before country names.
After να (na) the negative is μην (min), not δεν (dhen): για να μην έχει κίνηση (ya na min ékhi kínisi = so there's no traffic).
Θα βρέξει (tha vréksi = it will rain) – no 'it' anywhere: the verb alone is the full sentence for weather.
Weather often uses κάνει: κάνει ζέστη (káni zésti = it's hot, lit. it makes heat).
Θα αργήσει (tha aryísi = it will be late) – being late is a verb in Greek, so 'be' disappears into one word.
Αν + future-type form: αν δεν τρέξουμε (an dhen tréksume = if we don't run).
No 'a' before professions: θα γίνει καλή γιατρός (tha yíni kalí yatrós) – lit. 'she'll become good doctor', no article needed.
Θα δούμε τι θα γίνει (tha dhúme ti tha yíni = we'll see what will happen) – Greek keeps the future in both halves where English switches to 'happens'.
Θα ζητήσω αύξηση από το αφεντικό (tha zitíso áfksisi apó to afendikó) – you ask something FROM someone in Greek, not ask someone for it.
Μέχρι αργά (mékhri arghá = until late) – duration, so present-type form after θα (tha).
Παίρνω ρεπό (pérno repó = take a day off) – ρεπό never changes form.
Θα πάμε να δούμε (tha páme na dhúme = we'll go see) – να chains the two verbs.
Πίτα (píta) here is a savory filo pie – like τυρόπιτα (tirópita) or σπανακόπιτα (spanakópita) – not flatbread.
Στο εξωτερικό (sto eksoterikó = abroad, lit. in the outside).
Θα βαφτίσουμε (tha vaftísume = we'll baptize) announces a big family event – traditionally the godparent, not the parents, picks the baby's name.
Και here = too: θα έρθουν και οι θείοι (tha érthun ke i thíi = the uncles will come too).
Πριν + future-type form: πριν το καταλάβεις (prin to katalávis = before you know it).
Θα μάθουμε κολύμπι στα εγγόνια (tha máthume kolímbi sta engónia) – μαθαίνω (mathéno) means both learn and teach; 'to the grandkids' flips it to teaching.
Greek stacks negatives: δεν... τίποτα... σε κανέναν (dhen... típota... se kanénan) is correct, not clumsy.
Μπορεί να (borí na) is a fixed 'might/maybe' – different from personal μπορώ (boró = I can): μπορεί να βρέξει (borí na vréksi = it might rain).
Μην + verb = don't: μην ξεχάσεις (min ksekhásis = don't forget).
Κρατάω (kratáo) also = to last: θα κρατήσει πολύ; (tha kratísi polí? = will it last long?)
Το μέλλον θα δείξει (to mélon tha dhíksi = time will tell, lit. the future will show).
A reservation goes 'in the name', not under it: στο όνομα (sto ónoma = in the name) is the set phrase for giving your booking.
Έχει κόσμο (ékhi kózmo = it's busy, lit. it has people).
A present-tense question works as a polite request: μας φέρνετε; (mas férnete? = could you bring us?)
Παίρνω (pérno = take) is the usual ordering verb: τι θα πάρετε; (ti tha párete = what will you take?) is how waiters ask what you'll have.
